paper_title: Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A sparse terminal reward tells an agent little about its steps. Much of the missing information is implicit in the environment's dynamics, because each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A world model trained on real transitions can learn to predict what each action changes, but a predicted observation does not by itself show whether success has become more likely. With a binary terminal reward, PPO's critic makes this judgment by estimating the current policy's probability of success, but only for states the agent reaches. Our method, WM-PPO, elegantly brings the two together. For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. In the policy channel, comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages; in the value channel, their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels according to how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training. The policy, critic and world model all learn from the agent's own interaction, with no teacher or privileged information, and only the policy is used at inference. With a comparable number of real environment steps, WM-PPO raises success from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps before placing an object or committing to an answer.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Agents trained with reinforcement learning on multi-step tasks often receive only sparse terminal rewards, which provide limited feedback for learning. Yet each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. needed object is found, an operations precondition is met, or command is rejected, and the next observations record all these changes. When tasked with cleaning plate and putting it in cabinet, for example, an agent may find the plate and pick it up, but put it away without first cleaning it at the sink. The final reward marks the whole attempt as failure. It does not say which steps helped, or which other action would have left the agent better placed to succeed. World models learn environment dynamics by predicting how an agents actions change the environment. What predicted change means for success depends on the task and on what the current policy can accomplish from the resulting state. In text environments, an actions contribution to success is not necessarily reflected in how much the observation text changes. transition that produces very different textual observation may leave the chances of success unchanged: opening cabinet, for example, may reveal long list of objects unrelated to the goal. Conversely, small change in the environment may establish critical prerequisite or make the goal unreachable. Heating mug, 1 for instance, may produce only brief confirmation, yet satisfy necessary condition for task that requires hot mug. We therefore evaluate predicted transitions by their effect on eventual success. Fortunately, PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) already learns such valuation through its critic. The critic estimates the expected cumulative reward from state under the current policy, and its evaluation evolves as the policy learns. When agents must learn from sparse terminal success rewards, the critic offers feedback before the task outcome is known. Its values estimate the probability of eventual success, and changes across transition reveal how an action affects that probability. While PPO uses these estimates only through the advantages of executed actions, we apply the critic to the next states predicted by world model for the policys candidate actions (Figure 2). These estimates, which we call transition values, let us compare the policys candidates through their predicted consequences. Diagnostics on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) support this idea: selecting among the policys candidates using these values achieves higher success than direct policy sampling (Section 2). We therefore introduce WM-PPO, which incorporates this feedback through policy and value channels. At each state along the main training trajectory, the policy samples several candidate actions and executes the first as usual. The policy channel turns candidate comparisons into auxiliary advantages in PPOs clipped objective, while the value channel uses the mean transition value as an additional one-step target for the critic at the current state. These critic updates also affect the advantages used in subsequent policy updates. Since value estimation in LLM reasoning can be biased and yield unreliable comparisons between candidate steps (Yuan et al., 2025; Kazemnejad et al., 2025), WM-PPO calibrates both channels against real outcomes. For each training task, it collects one main episode and three branches, each trying different action at randomly chosen step. shared gate uses earlier branch outcomes to weight both channels according to the margin between transition values (Section 3). The design stays elegant: the world model is the only learned component added to PPO and reuses the real transitions collected during training. Real returns remain the critics main supervision. Training requires no teacher model or privileged information, and the policy acts alone at inference. Prior work also draws on signals beyond terminal rewards to improve language agents (Table 3 in Section 6). Some methods add observation-prediction losses during RL (Shrivastava et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Ran et al., 2026), while others learn environment dynamics before downstream policy training (Zhang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026a; Yu et al., 2026b). Distillation methods obtain finer feedback from teacher distributions or from models given hindsight observations or reference solutions (Agarwal et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). World models also provide imagined outcomes for action selection and refinement in WMA, ITP, and CoMAP, where they remain part of the deployed agent (Chae et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a,b). Internalizing the Future (Zhang et al., 2026b) learns from teacher-generated foresight traces. Its policy expresses confidence in an imagined plan before generating an action, and this confidence is calibrated against task outcomes to construct step-level advantages. ProActs MC-GRPO (Yu et al., 2026c) compares actions sampled at the same state using values estimated from simulator rollouts. WM-PPO instead evaluates candidates through their predicted consequences using world model and PPOs existing critic. Both networks learn from the agents own interactions, turning predicted state changes into feedback for policy and value learning. We evaluate WM-PPO on the simpler ALFWorld and on the harder ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022), whose tasks often require establishing intermediate conditions before the agent commits to an answer. The comparisons test whether learning from predicted consequences improves success for comparable amount of real interaction (Section 4). They cover PPO, its multi-turn refinements and group-based methods; structural controls that change one component at time; and auxiliary supervision from observation prediction, agreement and teachers. The main table compares 17 methods and variants, and the interaction-efficiency analysis places WM-PPO among 23 other methods and settings on ALFWorld and 20 on ScienceWorld. We then analyze how the two channels affect learning, and how the trained policy advances task (Section 5). Our contributions are threefold: Learning from dynamics by valuing predicted consequences. We show that valuing world2 model predictions with PPOs critic turns information implicit in environment dynamics into feedback that supplements sparse terminal rewards. Diagnostics demonstrate that these transition values support both action selection and policy improvement. Calibrating value-based feedback with real outcomes. To account for noisy critic estimates, we use outcomes of real branches to calibrate shared gate that weights both channels by how often comparisons with similar margins agreed with real outcomes earlier in training. The critics values thus reach both the policy and the critic itself as stable signal grounded in real outcomes. WM-PPO: transition values for policy and critic learning. We introduce two complementary learning channels: comparisons among transition values provide auxiliary policy advantages, while their mean supplies an auxiliary critic target. Only the policy is needed at inference. On ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, WM-PPO reaches PPOs success levels with fewer real interaction steps and achieves higher success at comparable interaction budgets.

sections.title: 2.1 Does the critic see the value of a state transition?
sections.content: We first test whether the critic can compare actions at the same state by valuing their real successors. At every step, the policy samples four candidate actions. Each distinct candidate is executed for one step in copy of the environment, and the critic values each resulting next state. The agent then executes the candidate with the highest-valued successor, which is expected to leave the greatest chance of success (Equation (3)). The policy is held fixed. Selecting by the critics value of the real successor raises success from 56.9% (majority vote over the four candidates) to 70.4%, gain of 13.5 points (SE 2.8, < 104; Figure 1a); executing single sampled candidate gives 54.4%. Most of this gain comes from valuing intermediate successors: control that selects candidate only when it completes the task immediately, and otherwise uses majority vote, reaches 59.5%. The critic therefore carries information about intermediate transitions that the agents own choices do not use. The reliability of this ranking depends on the gap between the critics values. Prior work reports noisy and initially biased value estimates that rank candidate next steps near chance (Kazemnejad et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025). At randomly chosen states, we executed each distinct candidate and estimated its success probability from three continuations. Of the 195 candidate pairs 4 whose estimates differ, the critic orders 57% correctly, and the median gap between its two values is 0.008. Ranking accuracy increases from 53% in the lower half of the critics value gaps to 71% in the top quarter. Among the 12 pairs for which one candidate succeeded in all three continuations and the other in none, the critic ranked 11 correctly (Figure 1b). Large value gaps identify the comparisons the critic orders most reliably. The reliability gate uses real outcomes to determine how much weight each margin should receive (Section 3.5).

sections.title: 2.2 Do predicted state transitions preserve this value?
sections.content: We next test whether learned dynamics make these values available for candidates that are not executed. world model replaces the one-step execution: separate LoRA adapter on the same base model, trained with next-observation loss on transitions that the same policy generated on 1,000 training games. For this diagnostic only, its data also include one-step executions of candidates the policy did not choose (48k transitions, 44% of them for such candidates); the world model of WM-PPO is trained on executed transitions alone. At each step, the world model greedily predicts the next observation of every distinct candidate, and the critic values each predicted next state. The agent selects the candidate with the highest value and executes it in the environment; the other candidates are never executed. Choosing by predicted consequences reaches 66.4%, 9.5 points above majority vote (SE 2.5, < 0.001; Figure 1a) and close to the 70.4% obtained with the true consequences. With the untrained base model as the world model, selection reaches 61.7%; the trained model is 4.7 points higher. Two controls examine why selection with true consequences performs better. When the true next observation is combined with the action list from before the step, as in the world models successor, selection reaches 65.3%. When newly revealed objects are removed from the true observation, it reaches 59.1% (Appendix C). Both the refreshed action list and the newly revealed content contribute to the gain. The predictions are exact for 99.7% of the held-out observations that follow from what the agent has already seen, but for only 26% of those that reveal objects it has not seen; for the latter, they still give prior over what will be found (Appendix C). In this diagnostic, predicted transitions preserve most of the selection gain obtained with real ones.

sections.title: 3 WM-PPO
sections.content: WM-PPO adds one learned component to PPO: world model pϕ trained on real state transitions to predict the next observation after an action. The policy πθ keeps PPOs clipped objective, and the critic Vψ learns primarily from real returns. At each training state, the world model predicts the consequences of the policys candidate actions, and the critic values the predicted successors. These transition values enter learning through two channels. Comparisons among the candidates supply auxiliary advantages for the policy (the policy channel), and the mean transition value supplies one-step target for the critic (the value channel). Small rollout trees provide real branch outcomes, and gate uses earlier branches to weight both channels by the reliability of their value margins. Section 3.1 defines the evaluation, Sections 3.2 and 3.3 the two channels, Section 3.4 the training loop, and Section 3.5 the gate. Figure 2 gives an overview, and Algorithm 1 summarizes one iteration (Algorithm 2 in Appendix B.1 gives the full procedure).

sections.content: Each iteration uses one batch of branched real rollouts. Actions and returns train the policy and critic, observed transitions train the world model, and paired outcomes calibrate the gate (Figure 2; Table 4 in Appendix B). Episodes and branches. Each iteration draws 64 training tasks. For each task, the policy plays one main episode, the chain, in which every step also records the candidates. The policy then plays three branches from the chain. For each branch, we draw step of the chain uniformly at random. Because the environments are deterministic, replaying the chains actions up to that step restores its state. We resample the policys first response at this state up to eight times, stopping when its action differs from the chains, and then continue the branch to the end. If all eight samples repeat the chains action, the branch continues with that action but yields no comparison. The policy proposed different action within eight samples in 6267% of the branches on ScienceWorld and in 4061% on ALFWorld. Each iteration therefore plays 256 episodes. sections.title: 4 Experimental Evaluation
sections.content: We test whether learning to value predicted consequences raises policy-only success for comparable amount of real interaction. All methods share 12-iteration PPO warm-up checkpoint and task order, and are evaluated as policies alone at fixed iterations. WM-PPO and PPO-160 use approximately the same number of real steps. WM-PPO, its policy-channel-only variant, PPO-160, PPO-256, Q-PPO and Wide-Tree-PPO have three training runs each, as does self-teacher OCSD on ALFWorld. WM-PPOs hyperparameters are set once on ALFWorld; baselines are re-tuned by rules fixed in advance when their settings fail (Section 4.1).

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Environments. ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) is the simpler environment. Its six household task types mostly follow the same routine: find an object, heat, cool or clean it when required, and place it at the requested location. The environment lists admissible actions at every step, leaving search for hidden objects as the main difficulty. We train on 3,553 games and pool evaluation over 140 seenroom and 134 unseen-room games. ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022) poses harder elementary science tasks. The 18 task types, fixed before training, all have oracle solutions within 40 steps. Eleven are procedural: the agent must first create or find an intermediate state, such as mixture, heated substance, connected circuit or an organism in another room. The other seven require choosing the right object among candidates. The agent must identify the relevant conditions in long room descriptions and express its actions as free text using 25 templates. Unparseable commands consume step, and focusing on the wrong object ends the task in failure. These dependencies make the value of state transition less apparent from the next observation alone: the agent must judge whether change establishes condition needed for later success. Appendix describes ScienceWorlds fixed training and evaluation sets. In both environments, the reward is 1 for completion within 40 actions and 0 otherwise, with no intermediate rewards. ScienceWorlds reported progress is part of the observation and is also predicted by the world model. Model and common start. All methods train LoRA adapters (rank 64) on frozen Qwen3-4BInstruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025) in non-thinking mode, with responses of at most 256 tokens. The shared PPO warm-up reaches 27.0% success on ALFWorld and 20.8% on ScienceWorld. Its real transitions also train the initial world model. Training then runs for 24 iterations on ALFWorld (1336) and 48 on ScienceWorld (1360). Comparisons. Table 1 lists the comparisons in three groups. The first group contains established ways of training the same policy: PPO at the two budgets, GRPO and GiGPO (Shao et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025), and three refinements of PPO for multi-turn agents, CAPO (Wang et al., 2026), SO-PPO (Li et al., 2026) and Turn-ratio PPO, turn-level form of GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025). The second group contains structural controls. WM-PPO (policy channel only) removes the critic target of Section 3.3; each other control changes one element of that variant. Wide-Tree-PPO keeps the trees and critic training but removes the auxiliary update. Q-PPO values candidates directly with Qω(st, y), learned from real returns. Fixed WM keeps the initial world model throughout training (Appendix D). The third group adds other auxiliary supervision to PPO-160. PaW (Lu et al., 2026) uses the published auxiliary next-observation loss to train the policy on dynamics, without evaluating predicted consequences for task success. Majority-vote labels use ungated self-training on the most common of four sampled actions (Zuo et al., 2025; Shafayat et al., 2025). Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024) uses frozen Qwen3-32B teacher (Appendix D.2). OCSD (Yang et al., 2026) uses the policy itself or the 32B model as teacher with access to the observations that followed the action. Hyperparameters across environments. WM-PPO uses its ALFWorld hyperparameters unchanged on ScienceWorld, adapting the prompts and the world models context and output lengths (Appendix B). Baselines also start from their ALFWorld settings and follow pre-set re-tuning rules if those settings fail. CAPO, SO-PPO and PaW required re-tuning (Appendix D). Interaction budgets. sections.title: 4.2 Policy-only Task Performance
sections.content: Higher success at comparable real interaction. On ALFWorld at iteration 36, WM-PPO succeeds on 87.5% of the evaluation games under greedy decoding and on 87.8% under pass@1 evaluation  (Table 2)  ; WM-PPO (policy channel only) reaches 88.4% and 89.4%. PPO-160, whose budget of real steps is matched by design, reaches 63.5% and 71.0%, and every run of either variant is above every PPO-160 run. The supplementary PPO-256, with about 50% more real steps, reaches 83.1% and 84.8%, also significantly lower in the per-game comparison. On ScienceWorld at iteration 60, using the hyperparameters from ALFWorld, WM-PPO reaches 52.9% greedy and 51.6% pass@1 success, against 39.3% and 42.6% for PPO-160 (p < 0.001). Every WM-PPO run (50.454.9% greedy) is above every PPO-160 run (37.740.5%). PPO-256, with 22% more real steps, is 9.2 points lower under greedy decoding and 8.0 points lower for pass@1 (p < 0.001). GRPO and GiGPO remain well below WM-PPO in both environments. They stay below when drawing 40 tasks of 4 episodes each, which covers 91% of the ScienceWorld variations (GiGPO on ScienceWorld only; Appendix E). ScienceWorld separates the strongest methods. On the simpler ALFWorld, CAPO, SO-PPO, Turn-ratio PPO, PaW and the two WM-PPO variants cluster at 85.488.4% greedy success, approaching the environments ceiling. This leaves limited room for success rates to distinguish the methods. The two WM-PPO variants have the highest greedy success, and adding the value channel gives no further gain at this level (87.5% against 88.4%, not significant). Under pass@1, WM-PPO (policy channel only) is ahead of CAPO by 2.7 points, SO-PPO by 6.3 (p < 0.001) and Turn-ratio PPO by 4.4 (p = 0.002), and the full method is 4.7 points ahead of SO-PPO (p = 0.01). ScienceWorld, with its greater demands on intermediate conditions, gives clearer separation. WMPPO reaches 52.9% greedy success against 46.5% for the best of SO-PPOs three settings, the strongest baseline: gain of 6.5 points (p = 0.004). The lead under pass@1 is 2.2 points. Here, the value channel adds 5.8 greedy and 4.4 pass@1 points to the policy channel alone (p < 0.001; Section 5.2). The PPO refinements change how executed actions are credited; WM-PPO adds comparisons with unexecuted actions and critic target built from them. PaW reaches 85.4% success on ALFWorld, 2.1 points below WM-PPO. On ScienceWorld, the single run with its best of three loss weights reaches 35.6%, broadly at PPO-160s level and slightly below its 39.3%. WM-PPO is 17.4 points higher (p < 0.001). WM-PPO uses the predicted observations to evaluate which consequences matter for task success. Higher success than the tested teacher-based methods. OPD and OCSD use teachers to supply feedback finer than final 0/1 reward. Self-teacher OCSD improves PPO-160 to 83.0% greedy and 82.7% pass@1 success on ALFWorld over three runs; WM-PPO remains 4.5 and 5.1 points higher (p = 0.003 and < 0.001). On ScienceWorld, self-teacher OCSD is 5.2 points below PPO-160 under greedy decoding (p = 0.02), level with it for pass@1, and 18.8 and 7.9 points below WM-PPO. The teachers judgment separates valid from invalid actions on ALFWorlds short observations (AUC 0.80), but is inverted on ScienceWorlds long descriptions (AUC 0.25 and 0.21; Appendix D.2). With the 32B teacher, OCSD reaches 70.1% pass@1 on ALFWorld and is level with PPO-160 on ScienceWorld. Standard OPD ends below PPO-160 in both environments (Appendix D.2). Ungated majority-vote labels reinforce the policys repeated choices without information about consequences; success falls to 17.2% on ALFWorld and 25.0% on ScienceWorld. WM-PPO outperforms these methods using world model and critic trained on the agents own interaction. Performance across runs. sections.title: Interaction Efficiency
sections.content: No other method achieves higher success with fewer real steps. Figure 4 compares each methods success and real interaction. On ALFWorld, 18 of the 23 other methods lie in the region below and to the right of the evaluated checkpoints of the two WM-PPO variants; on ScienceWorld, 18 of 20 lie below and to the right of WM-PPOs checkpoints. The methods outside the region used fewer real steps but reached lower success: on ALFWorld, CAPO (with two clipping ranges), Turn-ratio PPO, OCSD and PaW; on ScienceWorld, the tuned SO-PPO and OCSD with the 32B teacher. PPO-256 uses 150k real steps against WM-PPOs 102k on ALFWorld and 156k against 128k on ScienceWorld, and it ends below WM-PPO in both environments. The same success takes fewer real steps than with PPO. Figure 13 in Appendix plots success against real interaction; Table 14 reports each runs first evaluated checkpoint above reference success. By iteration 36 on ALFWorld, the three WM-PPO runs have passed 80% success after 69k97k real steps and the three runs with the policy channel only after 67k84k, against 129k141k for PPO-256. No PPO-160 run has reached 80% by this iteration. The PPO refinements rise fastest early: CAPO and Turn-ratio PPO pass 80% after 63k and 64k real steps. WM-PPO reaches their level by iterations 3036, and the two variants end with the highest success at iteration 36. On ScienceWorld, WM-PPO separates from PPO-160 after about 30k real steps, and the gap widens to about 6 points by 100k. Its runs pass 45% after 94k120k real steps and the tuned SO-PPO after 97k, whereas no PPO-160 run passes 45% within its 108k118k steps. The gap grows over training, in step with the reliability of the comparisons (Section 5.1). 17 Figure 5: Agreement of preferences with real outcomes (ScienceWorld). Computation. Serving and training the world model takes additional GPUs during training. At comparable real steps, an iteration therefore takes 1.31.6 times as long as for PPO-160 in wall-clock time and uses 2.73.8 times as many GPU-hours (Appendix E.5). This cost stays in training, where the world model and the critic extract the information implicit in environment dynamics; at inference the policy acts alone, without the extra models and GPUs of agents that keep world model (Chae et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a,b). The additional computation lets WM-PPO learn more from each real state transition, tradeoff that is useful when interaction is slow or costly.

sections.title: 5 Understanding the Gains
sections.content: A transition value estimates the current policys chance of success after candidate action (Equation (6)). This section examines whether these values identify choices that determine task success, how the policy and critic learn from them, and how the trained policy behaves as result.

sections.title: 5.1 Valuing Predicted State Transitions
sections.content: Section 2.1 showed that large value gaps identify comparisons the critic orders more reliably. This pattern persists during online training with predicted successors. Late in ScienceWorld training, the preferred action has the better outcome in 84% of branch pairs with different real outcomes in the largest margin bin, while the smaller bins are close to chance (Figure 5a; Table 20). What large margin means. large margin indicates large estimated difference in the current policys chances of success after the candidate actions. Such difference can arise when an action 18 Figure 6: Online updates maintain prediction quality as the policy learns (ScienceWorld). WM-PPO (policy channel only) and Fixed WM start from the same world model. (a) Exact nextobservation prediction on executed steps. (b) Recall of episode endings. (c) Greedy success during training on dev and test games. Each model is evaluated on its policys visited states, in windows of three iterations plotted at the last iteration. Band: range of three online runs; Fixed WM: one run; dotted gray line: mean of three PPO-160 runs. commits the agent to choice that prevents later completion. For example, ScienceWorld task requires focusing on non-living thing and moving it into box. Focusing on air leaves the episode running, but air cannot be moved into the box. Across the three runs, the critics value the predicted successor of focusing on air at 0.030.34, compared with 0.540.80 for going to the hallway. None of the 24 real continuations after focusing on air succeeds, whereas 19 of 24 succeed after going to the hallway. Such decisive choices make up growing part of the largest bin. Its share of pairs with different real outcomes grows from 14% early in training to 33% later, and its realized gain per pair from +0.08 to +0.22  (Table 19)  , which keeps its gate weight high (Section 5.2). Predicting successors improves candidate comparisons. Since transition value approximates an action value, directly learning network is natural alternative. The relation from Equation (5), ˆqt(a) Qπ(st, a) = E(cid:2)V π(st+1) (cid:12) (cid:12) st, at = a(cid:3), allows either direct estimate of Qπ or an estimate through the actions successor. Q-PPO tests the first route by adding network Qω(st, y) trained on executed actions returns. It replaces the world model and critics candidate evaluation while retaining the candidates, margins, gate and auxiliary update of WM-PPO (policy channel only). The world model can also learn from the next observation at every executed step, including those in failed episodes. Predicting successors therefore lets the evaluation use supervision about what actions change as well as the returns used to learn value. In ScienceWorlds largest margin bin, WM-PPO (policy channel only), which differs from Q-PPO only in how candidates are valued, favors the successful action in 85% of training branch pairs with different real outcomes, against 76% for Q-PPO  (Table 20)  . On shared pool of candidates, the comparisons using the world model are also more accurate at large margins (Figure 5b). Online updates preserve prediction quality on ScienceWorld. As the policy learns, it visits new states and proposes different actions, so the world model must keep learning from the resulting transitions. With fixed world model, prediction accuracy declines as the policy changes (Figure 6a). This decline also affects candidate evaluation: late in training, the Fixed WM runs largest-margin agreement is 5364%, against 8893% for the online run with the same seed (Appendix F.1).

sections.title: 5.2 Learning from Transition Values
sections.content: The comparisons supply information that additional branches alone do not. Wide-Tree-PPO keeps the trees and critic of WM-PPO (policy channel only) but drops the auxiliary update; across three runs per method, the policy-channel-only variant exceeds it in success by 10.0 percentage points on ALFWorld and 6.3 on ScienceWorld  (Table 2)  . single offline update on these comparisons alone also improves the policy (Section 2.3). The value channel adds feedback for the critic. Training the critic toward the mean transition value qt changes how it values the next rounds predicted successors, and hence the preferences used in later policy updates. In ScienceWorld iterations 1336, the largest-margin comparisons favor the successful action in 7882% of branch pairs with different outcomes, against 7174% with the policy channel only (Figure 7b). sections.title: 5.3 How the Policy Advances the Task
sections.content: The trained WM-PPO policy more often completes prerequisites before taking the action that depends on them. ALFWorld. WM-PPO more often processes an object before placing it. Its gain over PPO-160 is largest on tasks that require heating, cooling or cleaning before placement: 31.5 points, against 21.5 on plain placing (Figure 10a). The action order helps explain this difference. On processing tasks, WM-PPO places the object before processing it in 17% of episodes in which the object was picked up, against 41% for PPO-160 (Appendix F.5). In the mug-heating game, both policies find the mug; WM-PPO takes it to the microwave, whereas PPO-160 puts it into the cabinet unheated and fails (Figure 11a). PPO-256 also learns the processing order with more interaction; WM-PPO learns it within PPO-160s budget (Section 4.3). ScienceWorld. WM-PPO is more successful on tasks that require intermediate steps and less often commits to an answer before meeting its prerequisites. On the procedural games, it reaches 46.3% success, against 29.6% for PPO-160 (Figure 10c). An accepted focus command commits the agent to an answer, so its timing reveals whether the necessary conditions have been met. On these games, premature focus occurs in 22.0% of WM-PPOs episodes, against 28.7% for PPO-160 (Figure 10d). The living-thing task illustrates the difference: WM-PPO goes outside and brings baby beaver to the box, while PPO-160 focuses on fruit in the starting room and fails (Figure 11b). 22 Figure 11: Two evaluation games played greedily by the final policies; highlighted: decisive steps. sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Language agents can draw on information beyond the terminal reward in several ways. Table 3 compares the main approaches by what is predicted, how it is evaluated, where the resulting signal enters training, and what the deployed agent needs. Observation prediction and dynamics learning. ECHO, PaW and DGS-WM use real observations as auxiliary prediction targets during RL, so the policys own parameters are also trained to predict what its actions produce (Shrivastava et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Ran et al., 2026). DGS-WM keeps the observation fragments that best support the policys real next response, which favors decision-relevant content, but this selection score does not estimate eventual success. Other methods learn the dynamics before task-level policy training. Early Experience offers next-state prediction as warm-up before imitation, and alternatively mixes self-reflection rationales into imitation (Zhang et al., 2026a); SPA writes true states into the policys reasoning before RL (Chen et al., 2026a); and RWML rewards predictions that are close to the true next state (Yu et al., 2026b). In all of these methods, prediction is judged by how well it matches the real observation. WM-PPO keeps the world model separate and values each predicted change by its effect on task success. The two uses of world model could be combined. 23 Table 3: How information beyond the terminal reward enters agent training. : not part of the method. References are given in the text. Method Where the signal enters How it is evaluated What is predicted Deployed agent next observation, by the policy future or true states ECHO, PaW, DGS-WM Early Experience, SPA RWML WMA, WebDreamer change caused by each next state ITP CoMAP candidate multi-step imagined rollout imagined next state Internalizing the Future imagined plan (prospective rollout) ProAct (MC-GRPO / MC-PPO) (simulator transitions) OPD, OCSD Dreamer, MBPO, DreamGym WM-PPO imagined rollouts auxiliary loss on the policy supervised stage before RL policy policy action selection at test time context of the policy; SFT, then actor-critic RL supervised refinement similarity to the true state RL stage before task RL value model or prompted judge the policys reflection (training-free variant) the policys own reflection verbalized confidence, calibrated against outcomes immediate reward and random-policy Monte-Carlo state values token likelihood under teacher or hindsight self-teacher critic or returns on imagined data group advantages (MC-GRPO); TD(0) advantages (MC-PPO) distillation loss or rescaled token advantage training on imagined rollouts auxiliary step-level advantage in GRPO policy policy, model, evaluator policy and model policy and model policy with explicit foresight policy policy policy policy next observation of each candidate, by separate model PPOs critic on the predicted successor, weighted by real branches auxiliary advantage in PPO-clip; one-step target for the critic Predicted outcomes at decision time. WMA already pairs candidate actions with predicted consequences and value judgment. With the policy frozen, world model predicts the next observation of each candidate, value model scores it, and the best candidate is executed at test time (Chae et al., 2025). WMA also reports that scoring the predicted next state works better than scoring the action alone; Q-PPO makes the corresponding comparison inside training (Section 5.1). WebDreamer plans in the same way with an LLM simulator and prompted judge (Gu et al., 2025), and QWM selects robot actions by world-model search with learned Q-function (Dong et al., 2026). ITP lets the agent reflect on imagined multi-step rollouts before acting, either without training or after an expert warm-up and actor-critic RL that learns the imagination length together with the action; in both variants the world model stays in the deployed agent (Liu et al., 2026a). CoMAP, which is also evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, shares several design choices with WM-PPO (Liu et al., 2026b). Its world model is separately parameterized copy of the same backbone, retrained on the agents own transitions; its labels come from real two-branch rollouts; and gate decides when to refine. The policy drafts an action, reads the predicted next state and revises the draft after reflection. Training is supervised by expert or corrected actions, and the world model also learns from an EMA teacher that sees the real next state. The prediction thus enters the decision itself, and the world model remains part of the deployed agent. WM-PPO instead turns predicted consequences into training signals through PPOs critic, and only the policy acts at deployment. Learned foresight. Internalizing the Future combines future simulation and success estimation within single policy (Zhang et al., 2026b). Its mid-training and supervised fine-tuning use foresight traces that DeepSeek V3.1 writes from recorded trajectories, including their future continuations. During RL, the policy generates an imagined plan and confidence score before reasoning about the next action. calibration reward trains this score against the terminal outcome, and the scores of corresponding steps, normalized within the group, form an auxiliary step-level advantage in GRPO. The feedback therefore concerns the generated plan rather than comparison of alternative actions 24 from shared state. WM-PPO makes that comparison explicitly: the world model predicts the consequences of sampled actions, and PPOs critic evaluates the resulting states. Both learn from the agents own interactions, and their estimates provide feedback for policy and critic updates. At inference, the policy acts without an explicit foresight stage. Teacher and hindsight feedback. Distillation supplies token-level feedback from stronger or better-informed model. In standard on-policy distillation, the student generates its own sequences and teacher supervises its token distribution on these prefixes (Agarwal et al., 2024). OCSD, in its main configuration, uses the agents own earlier policy instead: it scores already generated tokens in matched replay contexts with and without the real later observations, and the score difference rescales the token update while keeping the sign of the original advantage (Yang et al., 2026). Its hindsight also comes from the agents own interaction; the difference is that OCSD re-scores executed responses, whereas WM-PPO predicts the consequences of candidates that were not executed. VASPO gives return-trained critic and self-teacher access to reference solutions during training and weights tokens by their judgments, on mathematical and logical reasoning (Wu et al., 2026). Like WM-PPO, it deploys the policy alone, but it predicts no state transitions. Section 4.2 compares WM-PPO with OPD and OCSD. Model-based reinforcement learning. WM-PPO learns dynamics from the agents own interactions and values predicted consequences to guide policy and critic learning. Dyna adds simulated transitions to learning (Sutton, 1991); World Models and Dreamer learn behavior inside latent model (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2020, 2025); MBPO branches short model rollouts from real states (Janner et al., 2019); MVE and STEVE build the critics targets from model rollouts (Feinberg et al., 2018; Buckman et al., 2018); and DreamGym replaces the environment of text agents with an LLM simulator (Chen et al., 2026b). Value Prediction Networks and MuZero learn models through values (Oh et al., 2017; Schrittwieser et al., 2020), and value equivalence judges model by the values it induces (Grimm et al., 2020). In WM-PPO, real rollouts provide every trajectory, the returns that are the critics main supervision, and PPOs advantages. The world model predicts one step for the policys candidates, and the critics values of these predictions enter learning as candidate comparisons and an auxiliary critic target. This target, the mean transition value, is related to value expansion (Feinberg et al., 2018; Buckman et al., 2018) and supplements regression on real returns. The gate checks the comparisons on real outcomes, in the spirit of value equivalence; the world model itself is trained by likelihood. Policy improvement over sampled actions. Valuing actions that were not executed, through learned critic, is the idea of all-action policy gradients (Allen et al., 2017; Ciosek & Whiteson, 2020). MPO reweights actions sampled from the policy by their estimated values, and AWR reweights the actions in its replay buffer by their estimated advantages (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2019); Muesli regularizes policy-gradient learning toward sampled actions valued with learned model (Hessel et al., 2021); Sampled and Gumbel MuZero improve the policy over sampled subset of actions with search (Hubert et al., 2021; Danihelka et al., 2022); and the MC-GRPO variant of ProAct executes candidates sampled at one state in the simulator and values each by its immediate reward plus Monte-Carlo continuations from random policy (Yu et al., 2026c). The auxiliary term of WM-PPO belongs to this family: it moves probability toward the best of the policys own samples. Its choices concern how to value these samples and how much to trust their comparisons. WM-PPO values candidates through their predicted successor states and PPOs critic, then uses outcomes from real branches to calibrate the reliability weights. Expert Iteration, AlphaZero, Dyna-Mind and the first stage of ProAct instead train the policy toward the output of search (Anthony et al., 2017; Silver et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2026a,c), whereas WM-PPO supplies scalar advantages for the policys own samples rather than target distribution. ProActs MC-PPO variant estimates state values through random-policy rollouts in the simulator, with 1,000 rollouts per state in our Sokoban comparison (Yu et al., 2026c). With comparable numbers 25 of real environment steps, WM-PPO reaches 87.0% success versus 77.3% for MC-PPO, significant gain of 9.7 percentage points (Appendix E.6). Value and credit signals for language agents. QLASS guides action selection with Q-network trained on exploration trees (Lin et al., 2025); SWEET-RL turns privileged turn-level critics ranking of sampled actions into preference pairs (Zhou et al., 2025); SPA-RL redistributes the final reward into per-step progress rewards (Wang et al., 2025); and process reward models score steps from step-level labels (Lightman et al., 2024). Agent trains on sibling pairs whose value gap exceeds fixed threshold (Putta et al., 2024), whereas the gate of WM-PPO measures which margins are reliable. VinePPO finds that PPOs value network ranks candidate next steps near chance and replaces it by Monte-Carlo estimates (Kazemnejad et al., 2025), consistent with the small-margin comparisons of Sections 2.1 and 5.1. Group-based methods compare episodes (Shao et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2026) or actions taken at the same state or history (Feng et al., 2025; He et al., 2026); PPO refinements change how advantages and ratios apply within turn (Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025); and majority-vote self-training rewards agreement with the policys most frequent answer (Zuo et al., 2025; Shafayat et al., 2025). WM-PPO complements these forms of credit assignment with learned comparisons of unexecuted alternatives.

sections.title: 7 Discussion and Limitations
sections.content: The value of predicted consequence depends on what the current policy can still accomplish from the resulting state. As the policy improves, the same successor can acquire different value. The world model learns which changes an action produces, and the critic relates those changes to task success using supervision from real returns. Evaluating alternatives in this way lets the policy learn preferences that few realized outcomes leave unresolved, including between candidates whose observed continuations end with the same reward (Appendix B.2). Large margins increasingly identify choices that change what remains achievable (Section 5.1). premature commitment can close off success, while step that establishes prerequisite can make it attainable. These are the decisions on which the comparisons are most reliable. The behavioral analyses show the corresponding change in the policy: it more often completes prerequisites before placing an object or committing to an answer. Gains are largest on procedural ScienceWorld tasks and ALFWorld tasks that require heating, cooling or cleaning before placement. They are smaller on forced-choice tasks, where correctness becomes apparent only at the end. What the world model predicts determines which part of comparison the critic must supply. Predicted endings supply outcomes directly, and comparisons between continuing successors rely on the critic. For the latter comparisons on ScienceWorld, the value channel raises agreement with real outcomes from 55% to 62% (Appendix F.1). On ALFWorld, no predicted ending settles comparison, so every comparison rests on the critic. The gate assigns only partial weights there (Figure 8). The value channel improves early candidate comparisons and the critics fit to real returns later in training (Figure 7; Section 5.2). WM-PPO trades additional prediction and evaluation during training for more learning from each real interaction. The benefit is higher success at comparable interaction budgets and fewer steps to reach PPOs success levels. The extra computation is confined to training; the deployed policy acts alone. Limitations. Our main evaluation covers one 4B base model and two text environments, with episodes limited to 40 steps. Branching and gate calibration require reproducible prefix, as in our deterministic environments, or saved state. branchs first action is sampled conditional on differing from the chains action. The update does not correct for this conditioning. single greedy prediction of the next observation does not represent uncertainty over possible outcomes. Longer-range effects enter only through the critic. Prediction errors can bias the auxiliary policy advantages and critic targets. Comparisons cover only the policys candidates, and many 26 small-margin comparisons receive little or no weight. Extending the benefit to these decision points remains an open problem.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: WM-PPO uses learned dynamics to evaluate candidate actions through their predicted consequences. world model trained on real transitions predicts each candidates next observation, and PPOs critic, trained on real returns, values the predicted successor according to the current policys chance of success. In the policy channel, comparisons between transition values become auxiliary advantages for the policys own samples. In the value channel, the mean transition value becomes one-step target for the critic at the current state. Real branch outcomes calibrate the weights of both channels. On ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the resulting policy achieves higher success than PPO with comparable real interaction. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. Unlike distillation, WM-PPO needs neither teacher model nor privileged information, yet it also surpasses the teacher-based methods we tested. When deployed alone, the policy more often completes prerequisite steps before committing to an answer or placing an object.

sections.title: A Prompts
sections.content: The policy and world model use chat prompts, each consisting of system message followed by one user message. Fields in braces are filled at every step. The policy sees the five most recent observationaction pairs; the action is the last <action> tag of its response (ALFWorld: one of the admissible actions; ScienceWorld: free-text command, judged by the simulator). Policy ALFWorld System: You are an expert agent operating in the ALFRED embodied household environment. User: Your task is to: {task} Prior to this step, you have already taken {t} step(s). Below are the most recent {k} observations and the corresponding actions you took: [Observation {i}: {o_i}, Action {i}: {a_i}] ... You are now at step {t+1} and your current observation is: {obs} Your admissible actions of the current situation are: [{admissible actions}]. Now its your turn to take an action. First reason briefly (at most two sentences) about the current situation inside <think> </think> tags. Then choose one admissible action for the current step and present it inside <action> </action> tags. At the first step the history line is omitted and the observation is the initial room description. Policy ScienceWorld System: You are an expert agent operating in the ScienceWorld environment, text-based simulator of elementary science experiments. User: Your task is to: {task} Rules: focus on OBJ declares which object the task is about and cannot be undone; focusing on wrong object ends the task as failure, so explore first and focus only on the object the task asks about. OBJ must be an object you can refer to now ( listed below); LOC is room name (teleport moves you there directly). Answering questions such as which one ... is done by focusing on the answer object. Prior to this step, you have already taken {t} step(s). Below are the most recent {k} observations and the corresponding actions you took: [Observation {i}: {o_i}, Action {i}: {a_i}] ... You are now at step {t+1} and your current observation is: {obs} Action templates: [look around, look at OBJ, look in OBJ, inventory, task, teleport to LOC, go to LOC, open OBJ, close OBJ, activate OBJ, deactivate OBJ, pick up OBJ, put down OBJ, move OBJ to OBJ, pour OBJ in OBJ, dunk OBJ in OBJ, mix OBJ, use OBJ on OBJ, connect OBJ to OBJ, disconnect OBJ, eat OBJ, flush OBJ, read OBJ, focus on OBJ, wait, wait1]. Objects you can refer to: [{objects}]. Now its your turn to take an action. First reason step by step (at most two sentences) inside <think> </think>, then give exactly one action inside <action> </action>. World model ALFWorld System: You are world model of the ALFRED text household environment. User: Task: {task} Initial observation: {room} History of steps so far: [Step {i}: observation {o_i}, action {a_i}] ... Current observation: {obs} Admissible actions: [{admissible actions}] Action taken now: {action} Predict the environments next observation exactly as the environment would print it, inside <obs> </obs>. 33 World model ScienceWorld System: You are world model of the ScienceWorld text environment. User: Task: {task} Recent actions: [Step {i}: action {a_i}] ... (the last 8 actions) Current observation: {obs} Objects the agent can refer to: [{objects}] Action taken now: {action} Predict the environments next observation exactly as the environment would print it ( action feedback, [Current room], [Inventory] and [score] lines), inside <obs> </obs>. The world models target is the true next observation inside <obs> tags. In ScienceWorld, our environment interface appends [task completed] or [task failed] at an episode ending, which the world model can then predict. The critic receives the predicted successor in the policys prompt format, with the prediction as its current observation.

sections.title: C Diagnostic experiments
sections.content: The diagnostics in Section 2 test whether the critic can compare actions by valuing their real successors, whether predictions preserve these comparisons, and whether the policy can learn from them. All use the policy and critic of the PPO run continued from the common warm-up to iteration 24 on ALFWorld (Section 2), the 274 evaluation games and per-game paired tests. Selection with true next states. At every step, the policy samples four candidates at temperature 1. Each distinct candidate is executed for one step in copy of the game. The critic values the history extended by the resulting observation and admissible-action list, and the candidate with the highest value is executed in the real game. In the peek control, candidate that completes the task is taken if one exists; otherwise the majority vote decides. Pairwise test. In each evaluation game, one state of the policys own episode is drawn at random; the draw is repeated with three random seeds. Every distinct candidate is executed and followed by three independent continuations of the same policy, and the fraction of successes estimates its value. For the 195 candidate pairs with different estimates, this order is compared with the order of the critics values of their true next states. World model for the diagnostic. The policy played 1,000 training games at temperature 1, executing the first of four samples; every distinct candidate was also executed for one step in copy of the game, which gives 48k transitions, 44% of them for unexecuted candidates. The world model is LoRA adapter on the base model, trained for one epoch with the next-observation loss. Accuracy is measured on 1,500 random transitions of the evaluation games, by category of the true next observation: observations determined by information already seen (71% of the transitions; 99.7% predicted exactly), observations revealing objects not seen before (20%; 26% predicted exactly, object F1 0.41), and Nothing happens (9%). Choosing with the true observation from which newly revealed objects are removed gives 59.1%, so hidden content affects selection. Where it matters, the world model still provides prior: it estimates whether the target object is present with an AUC of 0.81 (untrained model: 0.62). Offline update. The policy played 500 training games that are not in the world models data. At the 8,042 decision points with at least two distinct candidates, the label is the candidate whose predicted successor the critic values highest. One epoch of PPO-clip (lr 105, about 32k samples) uses the advantages of Equation (4) and no task reward. The KL divergence of the updated policy from the original is 0.017 with world-model labels and 0.033 with majority-vote labels. The evaluation samples at temperature 1, twice per game, without the world model. Inference-time lookahead on trained policies. Table 6 applies the selection test of Section 2.1 to trained ALFWorld policies on the 274 evaluation games. At every step, the policy samples four responses at temperature 1. pass@1 executes the first, which is the standard evaluation (three runs). Majority of 4 executes the most frequent action. True next state executes each distinct candidate for one step in copy of the game, values each extended history with the policys own critic of the same iteration, and executes the candidate with the highest value. sections.title: D Baselines
sections.content: D.1 Budgets, methods and tuning Budgets. PPO-160: 160 tasks 1 episode per iteration; PPO-256: 256 tasks 1; Wide-Tree-PPO, Q-PPO and Fixed WM: WM-PPOs trees (64 tasks (1 chain + 3 branches)); group methods: 20 tasks 8 episodes, also 40 tasks 4 for GRPO and, on ScienceWorld, GiGPO (Tree-GRPO: WM-PPOs trees or 32 trees of 8 leaves, Table 7); PPO refinements and the auxiliary-feedback methods: PPO-160s sampling. All start from the warm-up checkpoint with the same task order. Methods. Wide-Tree-PPO: WM-PPO (policy channel only) without the auxiliary term, that is, the same trees, tree GAE, critic targets and sibling term, and the same ordinary PPO rows of the executed steps. Q-PPO: third LoRA adapter with linear head reads the history followed by candidate response and is regressed on the return below each executed step, plus the sibling term; it is initialized from the warm-up critic and replaces ˆq in Equation (6); candidates, margins, gate and auxiliary rows are unchanged. Fixed WM: WM-PPO (policy channel only) with world model that is never updated after its initialization; the policy and the critic are trained, and the gate and the auxiliary rows computed, as in that variant. In both environments it starts from the same initial world model as WM-PPO, trained on the warm-ups executed transitions (on ScienceWorld, predictions at iteration 13 are token-identical for 78 of 81 shared statecandidate pairs). CAPO (Wang et al., 2026): action-level critic and importance ratio. SO-PPO (Li et al., 2026): one geometric-mean importance ratio per turn with clipping-triggered normalization. Turn-ratio PPO: the GSPO-style turn-level ratio (Zheng et al., 2025) with narrow clip, as implemented in the CAPO code base (Wang et al., 2026). VAPO-lite (Yue et al., 2025): PPO-160 plus language-model loss (weight 0.1) on responses of successful episodes. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) and HGPO (He et al., 2026): step-level grouping by identical environment states and by history, ported from their released code. Tree-GRPO (Ji et al., 2026): tree-based group advantages on WM-PPOs trees. Majority-vote labels: PPO-160 plus four samples per step and auxiliary rows as in Equation (8) with the unique plurality action as the preferred one, weight 1, no gate; computed on PPO-160s episodes, their total auxiliary weight is about two to three times that of WM-PPO. Standard OPD (Agarwal et al., 2024): frozen Qwen3-32B in non-thinking mode, which shares the students vocabulary, computes the log-probabilities of the executed response given exactly the students prompt; every tokens advantage is the whitened GAE advantage plus clip(log πT log πold, 5), the reverse-KL reward of on-policy distillation, with coefficient 1. OCSD (Yang et al., 2026): the teacher, the policy of the previous iteration (self) or the same Qwen3-32B, computes the log-probability of the executed response with and without the next one or two observations of the episode, but not the current action; the PPO advantage is multiplied by 1 + 0.5 sign(A) tanh(/2), where is the difference of the two log-probabilities, on the 20% 39 least likely steps per episode, following the released implementation. All OPD and OCSD variants are built on PPO-160 and use its interaction. PaW (Lu et al., 2026): PPO-160 plus PaWs auxiliary next-observation loss on the policy with the published settings: the clipped loss with ρ = 0.2 on the tokens of the true next observation, applied to the 75% of transitions with the highest action uncertainty, the reward-adaptive weight following the papers formula (with the batchs mean episode return under PPO), and the papers 20 prediction prompts. Unlike the original full fine-tuning at learning rate 106, it trains PPO-160s LoRA at 105. Published results. Several of these methods report higher ALFWorld success in their own papers. Those results come from different base models, longer training and other budgets. Here, every method shares one base model, one warm-up checkpoint, one task order and comparable interaction budget, and is reported at fixed iterations. Tuning rules fixed in advance. With the published clipping ranges, CAPO (0.001) clipped about 97% of tokens and Turn-ratio PPO (3 104) about 85% on ALFWorld, so both barely learned  (Table 7)  . For each of the two, three larger clipping values were tried for one update on the iteration13 data. The rule chose the smallest value whose clipped-token fraction was at most 20%, or the largest value if none qualified: 0.3 for CAPO and 0.1 for Turn-ratio PPO. On ScienceWorld every method first used its ALFWorld setting unchanged, and only setting that diverged or lost the action format was re-tuned (CAPO, SO-PPO and PaW); WM-PPO keeps its ALFWorld hyperparameters unchanged. Table 8 lists the ScienceWorld settings. SO-PPO on ScienceWorld. On ScienceWorld, SO-PPO with its published clip of 0.2 had periteration KL of 0.070.14 from the first update (PPO-160: 0.010.02) and collapsed after iteration 36 (15.8% at iteration 60). The rule fixed beforehand was to take the largest of 0.1, 0.05 and 0.02 whose KL after one update on the iteration-13 data was at most 0.02, or the smallest if none qualified. All three exceeded the threshold slightly (0.054, 0.035 and 0.022), so 0.02 was used. For SO-PPO we also ran the clip of 0.1 chosen by the clipped-token rule of CAPO and Turn-ratio PPO. This run did not diverge (per-update KL at most 0.08), but its success peaked at 22.9% among the evaluated checkpoints (iteration 36) and fell to 4.2% at iteration 60, when 92% of its evaluation episodes ended at the step limit. The main table reports the best of the three settings, clip 0.02. The same SO-PPO with clip 0.2 did not collapse on ALFWorld and is reported with the published value there. CAPO on ScienceWorld. CAPO with its ALFWorld clip of 0.3 diverged on ScienceWorld at iteration 14, and with 0.1 at iteration 28 (per-update KL spikes of 0.150.33, zero success); the last value of the pre-set grid, 0.03, diverged at iteration 18. No setting of the grid remains, so the main table reports, for CAPO on ScienceWorld, the official evaluation of clip 0.1 at iteration 18, the checkpoint with the highest greedy success in the evaluations during training (21.5%; 20.1% at iteration 15, 16.9% at 21 and 9.5% at 24), without test against WM-PPO. In the official evaluation it reaches 21.1% greedy and 20.0% pass@1 success, after 12.8k real steps; the neighboring checkpoints reach 19.0% (iteration 15) and 19.4% (iteration 21) greedy, so the choice does not depend on which evaluation is used. Turn-ratio PPO and PaW on ScienceWorld. Turn-ratio PPO runs on ScienceWorld with its ALFWorld clip of 0.1. It did not diverge (per-update KL of 0.020.06, three to five times that of PPO-160), but its success stayed near 25% from iteration 21 on, below PPO-160; because only diverged settings were re-tuned, it keeps this setting.
